oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet for pulmonary arterial hypertension; it aims to improve exercise ability and delay worsening.
whatItIs: Ambrisentan is a prescription medicine taken by mouth as a tablet. It belongs to a drug group called endothelin receptor antagonists. Endothelin is a protein your body makes that tightens blood vessels. Ambrisentan docks at the ET-A receptor, one of the sites that protein uses, and blocks it. The brand name is Letairis, and generic tablets are also sold. US regulators approved it in 2007 as a new molecular entity. Chemically, it is a small man-made molecule, formula C22H22N2O4, weight near 378.
whatItDoes: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood to your lungs.
One trial listing describes it as increased pressure in the right side of the heart.
Ambrisentan blocks endothelin-1 from docking at the ET-A receptor, which widens narrowed lung vessels.
The label lists two goals in adults with PAH: improve exercise ability and delay clinical worsening.
The label also approves it with tadalafil, another PAH drug, to lower disease progression and hospital stays.
howPeopleUseIt: It comes as 5 mg and 10 mg film-coated tablets that the label describes as taken once daily.
The label says the tablets are not meant to be split, crushed, or chewed.
Some people start it together with tadalafil; trial listings describe that pairing as first-line therapy.
Researchers have also studied it in scleroderma, for blood flow in the hands and Raynaud's flares.
That scleroderma use is experimental, not an approved use.

commonSideEffects: Peripheral edema means swelling, usually in the ankles and legs. It was the most common reaction.
In 12-week trials, 17% of people on ambrisentan had that swelling against 11% on placebo.
Nasal congestion, sinusitis (sinus inflammation), and flushing were also more common than on placebo.
With tadalafil added, common reactions included headache, cough, anemia, indigestion, and bronchitis.
Most reactions were mild to moderate, and only nasal congestion rose with a higher dose.
Hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying part of red blood cells, fell about 0.8 g/dL on average in those trials.
seriousSigns: Fluid retention has needed a diuretic or hospital care for worsening heart failure in some people.
Anemia severe enough to need a blood transfusion has been reported after approval.
Swelling of the face, lips, or throat, called angioedema, and rash have been reported.
Low blood pressure with symptoms has been reported after approval.
Sudden fluid in the lungs soon after starting can point to a rare vein disease, PVOD.
Sperm counts fell in animal studies, and the label says sperm production may be affected.
Serious birth defects are possible if the drug is used during pregnancy.
Liver enzyme rises have been reported, and the label says other causes were often found.
whoShouldAvoid: Pregnancy is a listed contraindication, meaning the drug should not be used at all.
People with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis should not take it, including those with WHO Group 3 PAH.
The label does not recommend it for people with moderate or severe liver impairment.
While breastfeeding, the label says to choose either the drug or breastfeeding.
Starting it is not recommended if you already have significant anemia.
Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established.

interactions: Cyclosporine, an immune-suppressing drug, raised ambrisentan blood levels about two-fold in healthy volunteers.
When cyclosporine is taken at the same time, the label limits ambrisentan to 5 mg once daily.
The label's interaction section names cyclosporine; tadalafil appears as a partner drug, not an interaction risk.
pregnancyAndChildren: Ambrisentan can cause serious birth defects and must not be used during pregnancy. That warning sits in a boxed warning, the strongest kind the FDA uses. Labels call for a negative pregnancy test before starting if you can become pregnant. Effective birth control is called for during treatment and for one month after stopping. It is not known whether the drug passes into breast milk. The label says to stop either breastfeeding or the medicine. Safety and effectiveness in children are not established. In juvenile rats given high doses, brain weight dropped slightly, with no changes seen in behaviour or tissue.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether the drug's strong preference for ET-A over ET-B receptors matters to patients is not known.
It is not known whether ambrisentan gets into human breast milk.
Human pregnancy data are thin, and the label says they cannot give a reliable risk estimate.
Why hemoglobin falls on this drug is unknown, and it does not appear to come from bleeding.
Liver enzyme rises have been reported without a clear explanation, and other causes were often present.
The label reports treatment exposure up to 4 years, so longer-term effects are not well described.
It is not approved for scleroderma or Raynaud's, and no benefit there is established.

summary: This record covers what ambrisentan is, its approved use, recorded side effects, interactions and pregnancy concerns, plus evidence gaps.
